project.name: Nook (ft_transcendence)
project.description: Nook, a social platform for the 1337/42 school community with chat (DMs and groups with channels), profiles, friends and search, built as microservices (Next.js client, NestJS user and chat services) behind an Nginx HTTPS proxy. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: What Nook Is
tour.description: The root README is only a placeholder, so the real overview lives in docs/. PROJECT_CONTEXT.md describes Nook's vision as a social platform for the 1337/42 community, its four product spaces (Feed, Chat, Play, Profile) and the 42 delivery constraints, while docs/README.md indexes the client, user-service, chat-service and infrastructure docs you will meet throughout this tour.

tour.title: The Compose Topology
tour.description: Everything runs as one Docker Compose stack: Nginx, separate PostgreSQL databases for users and chat, RabbitMQ, MinIO, the two NestJS services and the Next.js client. Healthchecks gate startup ordering so services only start once their dependencies are ready. COMPOSE.md explains the envs/ and volumes/ conventions and first-startup steps such as JWT key generation, giving you the map of the microservices before diving into code.
tour.languageLesson: In Docker Compose, `depends_on` combined with `condition: service_healthy` waits for a dependency's healthcheck to pass rather than merely for its container to start, which avoids services crashing while a database is still initializing.

tour.title: The Nginx HTTPS Gateway
tour.description: The browser reaches the stack through the Nginx image, which serves HTTPS on port 443 (and 9443 for MinIO) using its default.conf proxy config and a custom entrypoint script. The user-service Dockerfile shows how a backend boots in the stack: it generates the Prisma client, compiles, then at startup runs prisma migrate deploy and seeds the superadmin before launching dist/main.js as the non-root node user.

tour.title: User Data Model
tour.description: Before reading the user-service logic, look at what it stores. The Prisma schema defines User, Friendship, Block, UserImage and the auth tables (AuthProvider, RefreshToken, OAuthState, TwoFactorAuth, RecoveryCode, AuthToken), and the init migration materializes them in PostgreSQL. PrismaService is one of the most depended-upon backend files: a PrismaClient subclass that connects through the pg adapter and follows the Nest module lifecycle.
tour.languageLesson: Prisma keeps a declarative schema.prisma as the source of truth; `prisma migrate` generates ordered SQL migration files from schema changes, and the generated client gives fully typed queries for every model.

tour.title: User-Service Bootstrap
tour.description: main.ts is the user-service entry point: it creates the Nest app, restricts credentialed CORS to trusted origins computed by browser-origin.ts, and installs a strict global ValidationPipe. AppModule then composes the feature modules (configuration, Prisma, events, auth, accounts, social and superadmin), and following its imports outward is the natural reading order for the rest of the service.
tour.languageLesson: NestJS organizes code into @Module classes whose imports, controllers and providers arrays build a dependency-injection graph; a global ValidationPipe automatically validates and transforms incoming DTOs decorated with class-validator rules.

tour.title: Authentication and Sessions
tour.description: AuthService is the broadest file in the user-service: local registration and login with bcrypt, GitHub and Discord OAuth with account linking, JWT access/refresh rotation, email verification and password reset. Refresh tokens live in an HTTP-only cookie managed by session-cookie.ts, while access tokens are sent as Bearer headers and verified by AccessTokenGuard, which protects the authenticated routes you will see next.

tour.title: Accounts and Social Graph
tour.description: With authentication in place, the accounts module handles profiles, search, password changes and avatar/banner uploads processed by sharp into WebP and stored in Postgres. The social module manages friend requests and blocks, using per-user-pair locks inside transactions. API.md documents these REST endpoints, which form the contract the client consumes later in the tour.

tour.title: Publishing User Events
tour.description: Each service has its own database, so the user-service announces lifecycle changes instead of sharing tables. RabbitMqEventsService asserts the durable user.events topic exchange and publishes confirmed created/updated/deleted events carrying a profile snapshot. RABBITMQ_USER_SYNC.md explains how the chat-service consumes them and its HTTP profile fallback, bridging to the second backend.

tour.title: Chat Data Model
tour.description: The chat-service owns a separate PostgreSQL database with ChatUser (a local mirror of users), Group, GroupMember, Conversation, ConversationReadState, Message and Reaction. CHAT_OVERVIEW.md walks through the chat MVP, from session reuse for authentication to Socket.IO broadcasting and RabbitMQ profile sync, and serves as a guide for the next two steps.

tour.title: Chat-Service Core
tour.description: The chat-service boots from its own main.ts, and ChatModule assembles the controller, service and gateway with the groups, presence and MinIO modules. Its global AuthGuard verifies Bearer JWTs for both HTTP and WebSocket contexts, reusing the session from the user-service. ChatService implements DM creation, unread counts, idempotent message sending and soft deletes, while UserEventsConsumer upserts or deactivates ChatUser rows from the events published in Step 8.

tour.title: Realtime, Presence, Attachments
tour.description: ChatGateway exposes a Socket.IO /chat namespace that authenticates sockets, broadcasts new messages to user rooms and relays presence changes from the in-memory PresenceService (ONLINE/AWAY/OFFLINE with idle expiry). For attachments, MinioService issues presigned upload and download URLs and verifies uploaded objects, while the MinIO image, compiled from a pinned upstream commit in a multi-stage Dockerfile, provides the S3-compatible storage.
tour.languageLesson: Presigned URLs let a client upload directly to object storage with a time-limited signature, so large files never pass through the application server; the server only verifies the uploaded object afterward.

tour.title: Client Shell and Session
tour.description: On the frontend, the Next.js root layout wraps every page in the Providers tree: next-themes, a TanStack React Query client and the AuthProvider. AuthProvider is the second most imported file in the graph; it holds the session in memory, restores it via the refresh cookie from Step 6, dedupes concurrent refreshes and retries a request once after a 401. The (app) route-group layout then wraps in-app pages in the AppShell sidebar.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router route groups like (app) and (auth) are folders in parentheses that share a layout without adding a URL segment, so /chat and /login can use different shells.

tour.title: Typed API Clients
tour.description: The client talks to the backends through these typed fetch wrappers for /api/auth, /api/accounts and /api/chat, mirroring the endpoints from the earlier service steps. They centralize response parsing and friendly error mapping, and the chat client also performs presigned-POST attachment uploads with progress via XMLHttpRequest, matching the MinIO flow from Step 11.

tour.title: The Chat Workspace
tour.description: Everything comes together in ChatWorkspace, the file with the highest fan-out in the project: it orchestrates the DM, friends and groups directory, infinite-scroll history, Socket.IO realtime messages and presence, attachment uploads and the details panels. The /chat page validates the conversation parameter and renders it inside a Suspense boundary, and the Button primitive, the most imported file in the graph, represents the shared design-system components used across the UI.
